questions.question: What distinguishes a complete key from a prefix that only leads to longer keys?
options: The root has more than one child
The final node has a terminal marker
The key uses a fixed child array
The path is stored in lexicographic order
questions.explanation: A reachable path proves the prefix exists. The terminal marker separately records that the path itself is a stored key.

questions.question: A Trie stores both car and card. What should deleting car do?
options: Remove the entire c-a-r branch
Clear the terminal marker for car and preserve the child path to card
Delete card first, then rebuild the Trie
Leave car searchable until compaction
questions.explanation: The path is shared. Deletion clears car's terminal state and prunes only nodes that are childless, non-terminal, and no longer needed.

questions.question: Why can autocomplete cost more than O(prefix length)?
options: The root must be rebuilt for every query
The system must also visit descendants and produce bounded results
Terminal markers require a database lookup
Every prefix query scans all unrelated branches
questions.explanation: Reaching the prefix node is O(p), but candidate enumeration, ranking, and returned text add work proportional to the visited subtree and output.

questions.question: Which child representation is most likely to waste memory for a large Unicode alphabet with sparse branching?
options: A fixed array with one slot per possible unit
A map containing only present edges
A sorted vector containing only present edges
A compressed radix path
questions.explanation: A fixed array allocates every alphabet slot at every node, even though sparse nodes use only a few transitions.

questions.question: When is a hash table usually preferable to a Trie?
options: The workload needs longest-prefix matching
The workload needs ordered prefix enumeration
The workload mainly needs exact membership and not prefix operations
The workload must preserve shared prefixes
questions.explanation: A hash table avoids Trie node and pointer overhead when exact key membership is the main operation and prefix traversal adds little value.

questions.question: Why must reads and writes share one normalization policy?
options: Normalization determines the allocator page size
Different canonical forms can create separate paths for visually equivalent keys
Normalization removes the need for terminal markers
Every normalized key has the same length
questions.explanation: If equivalent input is encoded differently across operations, insertion and lookup traverse different paths and can create unreachable duplicates.

questions.question: Which publication strategy best prevents readers from observing half of a bulk Trie rebuild?
options: Mutate the shared root in place without synchronization
Build and verify a new snapshot, then atomically swap its root or version pointer
Disable reads until every old snapshot is deleted
Write terminal markers before child edges
questions.explanation: An immutable or copy-on-write snapshot can be verified independently and exposed through one atomic pointer change, preserving a consistent view for readers.
